questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is given an eye drop during an ophthalmology exam that stimulates cholinergic (parasympathetic) activity in the iris. Which of the following effects is most consistent with cholinergic activation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A decrease in gastric acid secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: An increase in heart rate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Constriction of the iris

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dilation of the bronchial smooth muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasodilation of skeletal-muscle vascular beds

explanation.summary: Cholinergic (parasympathetic) activation drives 'rest and digest' effects, including pupillary constriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that cholinergic activation causes the iris to contract, producing pin-point (constricted) pupils. Parasympathetic tone promotes the rest-and-digest functions of the body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergic activation increases gastric secretions and acid production as part of digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholinergic activation decreases heart rate through M2 receptors, rather than increasing it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cholinergic activation increases bronchial contraction, not bronchodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skeletal-muscle vasodilation is not the cholinergic effect described; parasympathetic tone supports digestion and elimination.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A researcher studies a smooth muscle receptor that, when activated, signals through a Gq-type G protein. Which of the following best describes this Gq-GPCR pathway?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of cAMP production by adenylyl cyclase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Activation of IP3 and calcium release

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct opening of a ligand-gated sodium channel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of cAMP through protein kinase A

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of the adenylyl cyclase enzyme

explanation.summary: The Gq pathway signals through IP3/DAG and calcium rather than through cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that the Gq pathway differs from Gs and Gi because it involves calcium release and signaling via calcium-dependent pathways, activating IP3 and increasing cytosolic calcium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activation of cAMP by adenylyl cyclase is the Gs (stimulatory) pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gq is a G-protein-coupled receptor pathway, not a ligand-gated ion channel like the nicotinic receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting cAMP via protein kinase A describes the Gi pathway, not the calcium-based Gq pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibition of adenylyl cyclase occurs with the Gi pathway, not Gq.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man in septic shock is started on norepinephrine to raise his blood pressure. At therapeutic doses, norepinephrine has the greatest affinity for which of the following receptors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-1 receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-1 receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alpha-2 receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beta-2 receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Muscarinic M2 receptors

explanation.summary: Norepinephrine acts primarily on alpha-1 receptors to raise blood pressure and systemic vascular resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states norepinephrine has more alpha-1 effects than alpha-2 or beta receptors (alpha-1 greater than alpha-2), causing constriction of vascular beds and increasing systemic vascular resistance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-1 receptors are only minimally affected by norepinephrine at therapeutic doses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-2 receptors are less affected than alpha-1 at therapeutic doses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-2 receptors are minimally affected; norepinephrine is not selective for beta receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Norepinephrine is an adrenergic agonist and does not act on muscarinic cholinergic receptors.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with decompensated heart failure and poor cardiac contractility is given dobutamine to improve her cardiac output. Dobutamine produces its positive inotropic effect mainly by stimulating which receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-2 receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-1 receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-2 receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beta-3 receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dopaminergic D1 receptors

explanation.summary: Dobutamine is a positive inotrope acting through beta-1 receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states dobutamine has high affinity for beta-1 receptors, and this beta-1 effect increases cardiac contractility (positive inotropic effect) as well as heart rate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dobutamine does not have much alpha-2 effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-2 activity is mostly in the lungs and mediates bronchodilation, not the inotropic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-3 receptors are mostly in the urinary bladder and do not mediate inotropy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dopaminergic D1 receptors are targeted by dopamine in the renal vasculature, not by dobutamine.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: Which of the following neurotransmitters is released by cholinergic neurons to mediate transmission?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetylcholine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dobutamine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dopamine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Epinephrine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Norepinephrine

explanation.summary: Cholinergic neurons release acetylcholine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines cholinergic neurons as those that release acetylcholine (ACh) to mediate transmission at the autonomic ganglia and at parasympathetic effector organs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dobutamine is a synthetic drug, not an endogenous neurotransmitter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dopamine is not the neurotransmitter of cholinergic transmission described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epinephrine is released by the adrenal medulla into the blood, an adrenergic signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Norepinephrine is released by adrenergic neurons, not cholinergic neurons.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: During a physiology demonstration, activation of a specific adrenergic receptor in the heart increases the heart rate. Which receptor is most responsible for this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-1 receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-1 receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alpha-2 receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beta-2 receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Muscarinic M2 receptor

explanation.summary: Beta-1 receptors increase cardiac muscle contraction and heart rate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states adrenergic beta-1 receptors are Gs-type GPCRs that increase cardiac muscle contraction and increase heart rate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 receptors are mostly in the periphery and drive smooth-muscle (vascular) contraction, not heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-2 receptors are Gi-coupled and are not responsible for increasing heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-2 receptors mediate smooth-muscle relaxation and do not increase heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic M2 receptors decrease heart rate.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman develops anaphylaxis with wheezing and hypotension after a bee sting, and epinephrine is administered. Which receptor mediates the bronchodilation that helps relieve her wheezing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-1 receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-1 receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-2 receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dopaminergic D2 receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Muscarinic M3 receptor

explanation.summary: Epinephrine causes bronchodilation through beta-2 receptor activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that epinephrine has equal affinity for alpha and beta receptors and is helpful in bronchodilation through beta-2 activation in the lungs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 activation causes vasoconstriction and raises blood pressure, not bronchodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-1 activation increases cardiac contractility and heart rate rather than dilating bronchi.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dopaminergic D2 receptors act in the renal vasculature and do not mediate bronchodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic M3 activation causes bronchial constriction, the opposite effect.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A critically ill patient is started on dopamine. In addition to its cardiac effects, dopamine activates receptors in the renal vascular beds that produce local vasodilation. Which receptors mediate this renal effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cardiac beta-1 adrenergic receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dopaminergic D1 and D2 receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Muscarinic M2 cholinergic receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nicotinic nN ganglionic receptors

explanation.summary: Dopamine acts on D1 and D2 dopaminergic receptors in the renal vasculature to cause vasodilation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states dopamine activates D1 and D2 dopaminergic receptors, which are in the renal vascular beds and produce vasodilation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 activation (seen at higher dopamine doses) causes vasoconstriction, not the renal vasodilation described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-1 activation increases cardiac contractility rather than dilating renal vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Muscarinic M2 receptors act on the heart to slow rate and are not the renal dopaminergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nicotinic nN receptors are ligand-gated channels at ganglia, not the renal vasodilatory receptors.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with cardiogenic shock has poor cardiac contractility but is not profoundly vasodilated. The team wants an agent classified primarily as an inotrope to increase contractility rather than one used primarily as a vasopressor. Which agent best fits this description?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dobutamine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dopamine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epinephrine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Norepinephrine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phenylephrine

explanation.summary: Dobutamine is classified as an inotrope, whereas epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine are typically classified as vasopressors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states dobutamine increases contractility (positive inotropic agent) and is therefore classified as an inotrope, in contrast to the agents grouped as vasopressors.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dopamine is typically classified as a vasopressor in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epinephrine is typically classified as a vasopressor for its potent vascular effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Norepinephrine is classified as a vasopressor with potent effects on the vasculature.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylephrine is a pure vasoconstrictor (pressor) and is not the inotrope described.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: All beta-adrenergic receptors couple to the same class of G protein. Activation of a beta receptor therefore leads to which of the following intracellular changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased cAMP through Gi-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased intracellular calcium through Gq inhibition

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct sodium influx through a ligand-gated ion channel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased cAMP through Gs-mediated adenylyl cyclase activation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased IP3 and DAG through Gq-mediated phospholipase C

explanation.summary: Beta receptors are Gs-coupled and raise cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that all beta receptors are Gs-type GPCRs, and the Gs (stimulatory) pathway activates adenylyl cyclase to increase cAMP.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased cAMP via Gi describes alpha-2 and M2 receptors, not beta receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gq signaling raises calcium; beta receptors do not act through Gq to lower calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Direct ion flux describes nicotinic ligand-gated channels, not GPCR-coupled beta receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased IP3/DAG via Gq describes alpha-1 and M3 receptors.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A student is asked how nicotinic cholinergic receptors differ from the muscarinic and adrenergic receptors of the autonomic nervous system. Which of the following statements about nicotinic receptors is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are activated primarily by norepinephrine

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are Gi-coupled GPCRs that lower cAMP

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are Gq-coupled GPCRs that raise intracellular calcium

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are Gs-coupled GPCRs that raise cAMP

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are ligand-gated ion channels

explanation.summary: Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels opened by acetylcholine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick highlights that nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated channels activated by ACh, distinguishing them from the GPCR-based muscarinic and adrenergic receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nicotinic receptors are cholinergic and respond to acetylcholine, not norepinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gi-coupled cAMP inhibition describes alpha-2 and M2 receptors, not nicotinic channels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gq-coupled calcium signaling describes alpha-1 and M3 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gs-coupled cAMP signaling describes beta-adrenergic receptors, not nicotinic receptors.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A patient in shock is given a vasopressor to restore blood pressure. Which mechanism best explains how a vasopressor raises blood pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased bronchial secretions through cholinergic activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased vasoconstriction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced cardiac contractility that lowers cardiac output

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slowing of the heart rate through M2 receptor activation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasodilation that decreases vascular resistance

explanation.summary: Vasopressors raise blood pressure by increasing vasoconstriction and systemic vascular resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines vasopressors as agents that increase constriction of blood vessels; the resulting rise in vascular resistance increases blood pressure, which is useful in acute, hemodynamically unstable patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased bronchial secretions is a cholinergic effect unrelated to raising blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reducing contractility lowers cardiac output and would not raise blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Slowing the heart rate is a cholinergic (M2) effect and does not describe vasopressor action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vasodilation lowers vascular resistance and blood pressure, the opposite of a vasopressor effect.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension is started on clonidine. Which of the following best explains how this drug lowers his blood pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: It increases norepinephrine release from sympathetic nerve terminals

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: It raises cAMP in cardiac myocytes to slow the heart

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stimulates presynaptic alpha-2 receptors

explanation.summary: Clonidine is a central alpha-2 agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-2 receptors sit on the terminals of presynaptic sympathetic neurons in the brain. When clonidine activates them, norepinephrine release is decreased, reducing activation of CNS adrenergic receptors and lowering blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist, not an alpha-1 blocker; it does not act as an antagonist on vascular smooth muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clonidine decreases, not increases, norepinephrine release; increasing release would raise blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ACE inhibition is a separate drug class and is not the mechanism of clonidine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-2 receptors are Gi-coupled and lower cAMP; clonidine does not raise cardiac cAMP.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman in the intensive care unit is given intravenous phenylephrine to treat hypotension. Shortly afterward her heart rate slows. Which of the following best explains this change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of cardiac beta-1 receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct alpha-1 stimulation of the sinoatrial node

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased norepinephrine release in the brainstem

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reflex bradycardia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reflex tachycardia from arterial baroreceptor unloading

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 agonist-induced rises in systemic vascular resistance trigger reflex bradycardia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenylephrine increases alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction and systemic vascular resistance. This activates the baroreceptor reflex, causing a decrease in sympathetic outflow and therefore a fall in heart rate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phenylephrine is an alpha-1 agonist and does not block cardiac beta-1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The heart-rate change is a baroreceptor reflex, not direct alpha-1 action on the SA node.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phenylephrine acts peripherally on vasculature; it does not increase brainstem norepinephrine release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rising blood pressure loads, rather than unloads, the baroreceptors, and the reflex slows rather than speeds the heart.

questions.stem: Phenylephrine binds alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle. Which of the following intracellular signaling sequences most directly produces the resulting contraction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of guanylyl cyclase increasing cGMP

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct opening of voltage-gated potassium channels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gi activation decreases adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gq activation stimulates phospholipase C

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gs activation increases adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 receptors are Gq-coupled and signal through the PLC/IP3/calcium pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: The alpha-1 receptor is a Gq-type GPCR. Activation stimulates phospholipase C, which converts PIP2 to IP3. IP3 releases calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum, raising cytosolic calcium and driving smooth muscle contraction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: cGMP signaling promotes vasodilation and is unrelated to alpha-1 activation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Opening potassium channels would hyperpolarize and relax, not contract, the muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gi-mediated lowering of cAMP is the alpha-2 pathway, not the alpha-1 contraction mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gs/cAMP signaling is not the alpha-1 pathway and would not drive this contraction.

questions.stem: A patient uses an intranasal phenylephrine spray for congestion. Which of the following best describes how the drug relieves the congestion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of histamine receptors in the nasal mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibition of mucus-secreting glands via muscarinic blockade

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stimulation of beta-2 receptors relaxing airway smooth muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vasoconstriction of nasal mucosal vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasodilation that flushes secretions from the sinuses

explanation.summary: Phenylephrine decongests by alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction of nasal vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Direct stimulation of alpha-1 receptors on the nasal mucosa causes vasoconstriction of local nasal vessels. This decreases mucosal edema, producing the decongestant effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: It is an alpha-1 agonist, not an antihistamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It does not work through muscarinic blockade of glands.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phenylephrine is selective for alpha-1 receptors, not beta-2 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylephrine causes vasoconstriction, not vasodilation, and its effect is on vessel tone, not flushing.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant develops hypertension that requires pharmacologic treatment. Which of the following agents is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clonidine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methyldopa

choices.label: C
choices.text: Norepinephrine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxymetazoline

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phenylephrine

explanation.summary: Methyldopa is the alpha-2 agonist indicated for hypertension in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methyldopa can be used for all types of hypertension and is specifically indicated during pregnancy, where it is useful for patients who develop adverse effects or become intolerant to other commonly used medications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clonidine is an antihypertensive but is not the agent specifically indicated during pregnancy in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Norepinephrine is a vasopressor that raises blood pressure and would be inappropriate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxymetazoline is a topical alpha-1 agonist for decongestion and eye redness, not for hypertension.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylephrine is an alpha-1 agonist that raises blood pressure and would worsen hypertension.

questions.stem: Methyldopa is often called a false neurotransmitter. Which of the following best explains this description?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It competitively antagonizes norepinephrine at postsynaptic alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: It depletes dopamine stores in the substantia nigra, which reduces central sympathetic outflow

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases synthesis of norepinephrine from tyrosine by activating tyrosine hydroxylase

choices.label: D
choices.text: It irreversibly blocks reuptake of norepinephrine at the synapse by inhibiting the NET transporter

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is metabolized to alpha-methylnorepinephrine, which is released in place of norepinephrine

explanation.summary: Methyldopa is converted to a selective alpha-2 agonist that substitutes for norepinephrine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methyldopa is taken up into sympathetic nerve terminals and metabolized to alpha-methylnorepinephrine, a selective alpha-2 agonist. This metabolite is loaded into presynaptic vesicles and released in place of norepinephrine, so activating presynaptic alpha-2 receptors decreases sympathetic outflow and lowers blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: It acts as an alpha-2 agonist through its metabolite, not as an alpha-1 antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Its antihypertensive action involves sympathetic terminals, not dopamine depletion in the substantia nigra.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It substitutes for norepinephrine rather than increasing norepinephrine synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methyldopa is not a reuptake inhibitor; it is stored and released as a false transmitter.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man taking clonidine for hypertension reports a persistently dry mouth. Which of the following terms best describes this adverse effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extravasation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypersalivation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mydriasis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reflex tachycardia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Xerostomia

explanation.summary: Dry mouth from clonidine is called xerostomia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Xerostomia, or dryness of the mouth, is a common adverse effect associated with clonidine use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Extravasation refers to a drug leaking into tissue at an IV site, not to dry mouth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypersalivation is the opposite of the dry mouth seen with clonidine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mydriasis is pupil dilation, an effect of alpha-1 stimulation in the eye, not a clonidine dry-mouth effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reflex tachycardia is not the described symptom and is not a listed clonidine effect.

questions.stem: In addition to treating hypertension, clonidine is used as an adjunct for which of the following conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circulatory shock requiring vasopressor support

choices.label: C
choices.text: Persistent facial erythema of rosacea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nasal congestion from allergic rhinitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pupil dilation for a dilated retinal exam

explanation.summary: Clonidine's reduction of central norepinephrine makes it useful as an ADHD adjunct.
explanation.whyCorrect: By decreasing norepinephrine release in the brain, clonidine can help control unwanted behaviors in psychiatric conditions such as ADHD and Tourette syndrome, and it is used as an adjunct treatment for ADHD.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Circulatory shock is treated with alpha-1 vasopressors like phenylephrine, not clonidine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Facial erythema is treated with topical oxymetazoline, not clonidine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nasal congestion is treated with alpha-1 agonists such as phenylephrine or oxymetazoline.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pupil dilation is produced by alpha-1 agonists acting on the iris, not by clonidine.

questions.stem: Compared with norepinephrine and epinephrine, phenylephrine has a longer duration of action. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds alpha-1 receptors irreversibly

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a selective alpha-2 agonist that resists enzymatic breakdown

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is highly protein bound in plasma

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is not a catecholamine and therefore is not metabolized by COMT

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is rapidly recycled by neuronal reuptake

explanation.summary: Phenylephrine escapes COMT metabolism because it is not a catecholamine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike norepinephrine and epinephrine, phenylephrine is not a catecholamine, so it is not metabolized by catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT). This gives it a longer duration of action.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Its longer action is due to slower metabolism, not irreversible receptor binding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1, not alpha-2, agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes the longer duration to lack of COMT metabolism, not protein binding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Escape from COMT metabolism, not neuronal recycling, explains the longer effect.

questions.stem: During an infusion of intravenous phenylephrine, the drug leaks out of the vein into the surrounding tissue. Which of the following complications is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypotension at the injection site

choices.label: B
choices.text: Local skin necrosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Localized vasodilation and warmth

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reflex tachycardia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Xerostomia

explanation.summary: Extravasated phenylephrine causes intense local vasoconstriction and tissue necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peripheral extravasation of phenylephrine into surrounding tissue leads to excessive vasoconstriction, which can cause skin necrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Its alpha-1 action raises pressure and constricts local vessels rather than causing local hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phenylephrine constricts vessels; extravasation causes ischemia, not vasodilation and warmth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Extravasation causes a local tissue injury; the systemic reflex from phenylephrine is bradycardia, not tachycardia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Xerostomia is a clonidine effect, not a consequence of phenylephrine extravasation.

questions.stem: An ophthalmologist applies phenylephrine drops before a retinal examination. Which of the following effects makes the drug useful for this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corneal anesthesia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased tear production

choices.label: C
choices.text: Miosis from contraction of the sphincter pupillae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mydriasis from stimulation of the iris dilator muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced intraocular pressure by increasing aqueous outflow

explanation.summary: Phenylephrine dilates the pupil by stimulating alpha-1 receptors on the iris dilator muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stimulation of alpha-1 receptors on the dilator muscle of the iris causes mydriasis, which is why phenylephrine is used as a diagnostic tool in ophthalmologic investigations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phenylephrine is not a corneal anesthetic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes its ophthalmic use to pupil dilation and vasoconstriction, not tear production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phenylephrine causes mydriasis (dilation), not miosis (constriction).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Its ophthalmic role is pupil dilation for exams, not lowering intraocular pressure.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements correctly contrasts alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-1 receptors are presynaptic, while alpha-2 receptors are postsynaptic on vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alpha-1 receptors couple to Gq, while alpha-2 receptors are presynaptic and couple to Gi to reduce norepinephrine release

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alpha-1 receptors decrease cytosolic calcium, while alpha-2 receptors increase it

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors couple to Gs and raise cAMP

choices.label: E
choices.text: Alpha-2 receptors are widely distributed near the sympathetic terminal, while alpha-1 receptors regulate neurotransmitter release

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 receptors are postsynaptic Gq receptors; alpha-2 are presynaptic Gi receptors that curb norepinephrine release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-1 receptors are widely distributed in the immediate vicinity of the sympathetic terminal and are Gq-coupled, whereas alpha-2 receptors are presynaptic, couple to Gi, and regulate (reduce) the release of neurotransmitters such as norepinephrine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the locations; alpha-2 receptors are the presynaptic subtype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-1 activation increases cytosolic calcium through the Gq/IP3 pathway, not decreases it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-1 receptors are Gq-coupled and alpha-2 are Gi-coupled; neither raises cAMP through Gs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the roles; alpha-1 receptors are near the terminal and alpha-2 receptors regulate neurotransmitter release.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with agitation, chest tightness, and palpitations an hour after using an illicit stimulant at a concert. His pulse is 128/min and blood pressure is 182/102 mm Hg; his pupils are dilated and his skin is moist. Toxicology confirms cocaine. Which of the following best describes the primary action of this drug at the nerve terminal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct agonism at postsynaptic alpha-1 and beta-1 receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Displacement of monoamines from vesicles via VMAT2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of catechol-O-methyltransferase in target tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonselective blockade of DAT, NET, and SERT

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selective blockade of the dopamine transporter only

explanation.summary: Cocaine non-selectively blocks DAT, NET, and SERT, so monoamines accumulate in the synaptic cleft.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cocaine is an indirect-acting sympathomimetic that blocks the dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin transporters on presynaptic neurons. Preventing reuptake prolongs and amplifies monoamine signaling. Excess norepinephrine produces the tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, and diaphoresis seen here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Direct receptor agonism describes part of ephedrine's action, not cocaine's; cocaine raises monoamines in the cleft.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Disrupting vesicular storage through VMAT2 is a mechanism of amphetamines, not cocaine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: COMT inhibition is not cocaine's mechanism; COMT inactivates catecholamines that diffuse away from the synapse.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cocaine is not selective for DAT; it blocks DAT, NET, and SERT, and the NET blockade drives the peripheral sympathetic signs.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student takes oral amphetamine tablets to stay awake before exams. Besides competing with dopamine and norepinephrine for reuptake, the drug raises the cytoplasmic pool of dopamine and norepinephrine available for release. Interaction with which of the following accounts for this rise in the cytoplasmic pool?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Catechol-O-methyltransferase in nearby tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Postsynaptic beta-1 adrenergic receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Syntaxin within the presynaptic SNARE complex

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vesicular monoamine transporter-2 (VMAT2)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Voltage-gated sodium channels on the axon

explanation.summary: Amphetamines disrupt VMAT2 storage, moving monoamines from vesicles into the cytoplasm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amphetamines interact with VMAT2, causing dopamine, norepinephrine, and other monoamines to leave storage vesicles and enter the neuronal cytoplasm. This rise in cytoplasmic monoamines increases the amount available for release and amplifies sympathetic and CNS stimulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: COMT methylates catecholamines that diffuse out of the synapse; it does not hold the stored pool inside the terminal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Postsynaptic beta-1 receptors respond to released norepinephrine; they do not set the presynaptic cytoplasmic pool.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Syntaxin is a SNARE protein that anchors vesicles; amphetamine's storage effect is not described as acting on it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Voltage-gated sodium channel blockade is a property of cocaine, linked to its local anesthetic and cardiotoxic effects.

questions.stem: A researcher applies a toxin that blocks voltage-gated calcium channels on presynaptic nerve terminals and then stimulates the axon. The action potential still reaches the terminal. Which of the following steps is most directly prevented?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of norepinephrine to postsynaptic receptors already present

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fusion of vesicles and release of transmitter into the cleft

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methylation of norepinephrine by enzymes in surrounding tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reuptake of norepinephrine through the presynaptic transporter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synthesis of catecholamines from their amino acid precursor

explanation.summary: Calcium influx through presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels triggers vesicle fusion and transmitter release.
explanation.whyCorrect: When an action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal, voltage-gated calcium channels open and calcium enters. This calcium influx triggers vesicles to fuse and release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft. Blocking these channels prevents release even though the action potential arrives.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Postsynaptic binding follows release; with no calcium influx there is no released transmitter to bind.
whyWrongByChoice.C: COMT methylation occurs after transmitter has diffused away; it is not triggered by presynaptic calcium entry.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NET reuptake clears transmitter after release; it is not the calcium-triggered step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transmitter synthesis in the cell body or terminal does not require the calcium influx triggered by the action potential.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman develops palpitations and a blood pressure of 170/98 mm Hg after taking an herbal weight-loss product containing ma huang alkaloid. Its active compound acts on adrenergic signaling in two ways at once. Which of the following best describes its mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activates norepinephrine transporters to speed norepinephrine uptake

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocks alpha and beta receptors and prevents norepinephrine release

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blocks DAT, NET, and SERT without any receptor agonism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits norepinephrine reuptake while sparing receptor activation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulates alpha and beta receptors and releases stored norepinephrine

explanation.summary: Ephedrine is mixed-acting: direct alpha/beta agonism plus indirect release of stored norepinephrine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ephedrine, the alkaloid in ma huang, directly stimulates alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors and indirectly enhances sympathetic activity by releasing stored norepinephrine from presynaptic terminals. These combined actions produce broad sympathetic stimulation with cardiovascular risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activating NET would shorten norepinephrine signaling; ephedrine instead increases norepinephrine release.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Receptor blockade would lower, not raise, heart rate and blood pressure; ephedrine is an agonist and releaser.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pure reuptake blockade of all three transporters describes cocaine, not the mixed-acting alkaloid in ma huang.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reuptake inhibition alone is not ephedrine's action; it directly stimulates receptors and releases norepinephrine.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man who smokes methamphetamine daily is evaluated for paranoia and weight loss. A student asks why this drug is more addictive and longer acting than amphetamine despite a qualitatively similar mechanism. Which of the following best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of VMAT2 effects, limiting storage disruption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher lipid solubility, enhancing blood-brain barrier entry

choices.label: C
choices.text: Higher water solubility, permitting faster renal clearance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower affinity for SERT, sparing serotonin reuptake

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selective release of norepinephrine, sparing dopamine

explanation.summary: An added methyl group makes methamphetamine more lipid soluble, so it enters the brain more, releases more dopamine, and lasts longer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Compared with amphetamine, methamphetamine carries an added methyl group that increases lipid solubility and blood-brain barrier penetration. As a result it produces greater dopamine release, a longer duration of action, and a higher risk of abuse, neurotoxicity, and oxidative neuronal injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Its mechanism is qualitatively similar to amphetamine, which includes disrupting VMAT2 storage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Faster clearance would shorten, not lengthen, the duration of action; the structural change increases lipid solubility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methamphetamine has higher, not lower, affinity for SERT than amphetamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methamphetamine produces greater, not less, dopamine release than amphetamine.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman seeks help for compulsive cocaine use. Her physician explains that the intense euphoria reinforcing her drug-taking comes from dopamine accumulating in the mesolimbic reward pathway. Between which structures does this pathway run?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal medulla and sympathetic chain ganglia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cerebellum and the vestibular nuclei

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypothalamus and the posterior pituitary

choices.label: D
choices.text: Substantia nigra and the motor cortex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ventral tegmental area and nucleus accumbens

explanation.summary: Cocaine's abuse potential stems from dopamine accumulating between the VTA and nucleus accumbens.
explanation.whyCorrect: By blocking DAT, cocaine causes dopamine to accumulate in the mesolimbic reward pathway, particularly between the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and the nucleus accumbens. The resulting dopamine surge produces intense euphoria and reinforces drug-taking behavior.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The adrenal medulla converts norepinephrine to epinephrine; it is not part of the mesolimbic reward pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These structures do not form the mesolimbic reward pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This pairing is not the mesolimbic reward pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This pairing is not the reward pathway the lecture identifies for cocaine's euphoria.

questions.stem: An otolaryngologist notes that cocaine applied to the nasal mucosa numbs the area, an effect not explained by catecholamine accumulation. The same property contributes to the drug's cardiac toxicity in overdose. Which additional action of cocaine underlies both effects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of voltage-gated calcium channels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct agonism at beta-2 adrenergic receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Disruption of vesicular storage through VMAT2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of monoamine oxidase in terminals

explanation.summary: Cocaine also blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, giving local anesthesia and adding to cardiotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond blocking monoamine reuptake transporters, cocaine inhibits voltage-gated sodium channels. This property accounts for its local anesthetic effect and some of its cardiotoxicity, alongside the excess sympathetic stimulation from norepinephrine accumulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels trigger transmitter release; cocaine's anesthetic action is attributed to sodium channel blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Direct beta-2 agonism belongs to ephedrine and explains bronchodilation, not local anesthesia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: VMAT2 disruption is an amphetamine mechanism, not the basis of cocaine's numbing effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MAO inhibition is described for amphetamines, not as the basis of cocaine's local anesthetic effect.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man reports that he recently switched from snorting powder to smoking crack because the high comes on harder and faster. Which of the following best explains why the smoked form produces a more intense rush?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The free base binds the serotonin transporter more selectively

choices.label: B
choices.text: The free base is volatile and absorbed rapidly through the lungs

choices.label: C
choices.text: The salt form is destroyed by heat before reaching the airway

choices.label: D
choices.text: The salt form is more water soluble and dissolves in mucus

choices.label: E
choices.text: The smoked form is converted to a longer-acting metabolite

explanation.summary: Free-base (crack) cocaine is lipophilic and volatile, so it can be smoked and reaches the brain rapidly.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cocaine hydrochloride is a crystalline, water-soluble salt that is snorted or injected. Conversion to free-base cocaine, including crack, increases lipophilicity and volatility so it can be smoked. Pulmonary absorption delivers the drug rapidly to the brain, producing an intense rush that contributes to abuse potential.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Free-base conversion changes lipophilicity and volatility, not transporter selectivity; cocaine remains non-selective.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This does not explain the rush; the free base's lipophilicity and volatility permit rapid pulmonary absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Water-soluble cocaine hydrochloride is the form snorted or injected; it is not the smoked form.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No longer-acting metabolite explains the rush; the rapid pulmonary delivery to the brain does.

questions.stem: In an experiment, norepinephrine released from sympathetic terminals is tracked after it diffuses out of the synaptic cleft into the surrounding tissue. There it is inactivated by an enzyme acting in the tissue rather than within the terminal. Which enzyme performs this step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Monoamine oxidase (MAO) within the terminal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Norepinephrine transporter (NET)

choices.label: D
choices.text: SNAP-25 of the SNARE complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vesicular monoamine transporter-2 (VMAT2)

explanation.summary: COMT in surrounding tissues methylates and inactivates catecholamines that diffuse away from the synapse.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neurotransmitters that diffuse away from the synapse can be metabolized by catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) in surrounding tissues. COMT catalyzes the methylation of catecholamines, contributing to inactivation of norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: MAO metabolizes neurotransmitter within the nerve terminal; methylation in surrounding tissue is performed by COMT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NET carries norepinephrine back into the presynaptic terminal; it does not methylate it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SNAP-25 is a SNARE protein involved in vesicle docking, not catecholamine inactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VMAT2 loads catecholamines into vesicles; it is a transporter, not an inactivating enzyme.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with a long history of smoking methamphetamine presents with widespread tooth decay, fractured teeth, and enamel erosion. Which combination of factors best accounts for these dental findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bronchodilation, tremor, and insomnia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bruxism, dry mouth, and poor oral hygiene

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excess salivation, jaw rest, and frequent brushing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gingival overgrowth, vitamin excess, and fluoride use

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nasal septal perforation and recurrent epistaxis

explanation.summary: Meth mouth reflects bruxism, dry mouth, and poor oral hygiene in chronic methamphetamine smokers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic methamphetamine smokers often develop meth mouth: tooth decay, fracture, and loss with acid erosion. It results from bruxism (teeth grinding), dry mouth, and poor oral hygiene over the course of drug use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These are ephedrine effects and do not explain dental destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These would be protective; meth mouth results from dry mouth, grinding, and poor hygiene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These factors are not the described causes of meth mouth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Septal damage and nosebleeds are linked to snorting cut cocaine, not to meth mouth.

questions.stem: A pharmacologist compares two stimulants. Drug X raises synaptic catecholamines only by preventing their reuptake. Drug Y enters the terminal through monoamine transporters, empties storage vesicles into the cytoplasm, and inhibits the enzyme that degrades monoamines inside the terminal. Drug Y is most likely which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amphetamine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cocaine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epinephrine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Norepinephrine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tyrosine

explanation.summary: Amphetamines inhibit transporters, disrupt VMAT2 storage, and inhibit MAO; cocaine only blocks reuptake.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amphetamines enter presynaptic neurons through monoamine transporters, compete with dopamine and norepinephrine for reuptake, disrupt vesicular storage via VMAT2, and inhibit MAO. Together these raise cytoplasmic and synaptic catecholamines. Cocaine, by contrast, increases synaptic levels by blocking reuptake.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cocaine fits Drug X: it raises synaptic monoamines by blocking reuptake transporters, without VMAT2 or MAO effects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epinephrine is a catecholamine formed from norepinephrine in the adrenal medulla, not an indirect releaser.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Norepinephrine is the transmitter itself, not a drug acting on vesicles and MAO.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tyrosine is the precursor transported into adrenergic terminals for catecholamine synthesis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man dies of a cardiovascular event after taking several bottles of an herbal energy supplement from different brands. Analysis shows that the amount of active alkaloid differed widely between products. Which of the following best explains why such products led to fatal toxicity and regulatory action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contaminating cocaine caused nasal septal perforation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low ephedrine content caused withdrawal hypotension

choices.label: C
choices.text: Uniform ephedrine content caused gradual receptor blockade

choices.label: D
choices.text: Variable caffeine content caused inadvertent serotonin excess

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variable ephedrine content caused inadvertent high-dose exposure

explanation.summary: Variable ephedrine content in ma huang supplements caused unexpected high doses, cardiovascular deaths, and an FDA ban.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ma huang supplements contain ephedrine, and its content varies across products, so inadvertent high-dose consumption can occur. Its alpha- and beta-agonist properties can cause significant cardiovascular toxicity and death, and the FDA banned ephedrine-containing supplements.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Septal perforation from cut cocaine is unrelated to the toxicity of ma huang supplements.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The danger was unexpectedly high doses producing cardiovascular toxicity, not low doses causing hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ephedrine is an agonist and releaser, and the problem was variable rather than uniform content.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lecture ties supplement deaths to ephedrine's alpha and beta agonism, not caffeine or serotonin excess.
